title: Bor and the Borrowed Bloom
markdown:
The mountains breathed steam into a bruised twilight. Below them the Ash Meadows lay in soft grey dust, dotted with hardy flowers that had decided colour was still worth the trouble. This was Bor’s country. He was an ogre the size of a kind hill. His hands, shovel-broad, were careful with small things. His heart had the temperature of moss in shade.

He kept unusually smooth river stones. He kept, more carefully, Pipkin: a ram whose fleece was the colour of a storm thinking about it, eyes like dark earth that had learned patience.

Bor had borrowed a Whispering Bloom from Elder Ogre Grok, whose beard had reached the ground and stayed there. The flower unfurled with a sound like a sigh. The task was simple: return it before the Ash Meadow Festival. The difficulty was not the path. It was the being-seen. Honesty sat easily on Bor. Attention made his knobbly knees behave like saplings. He preferred to put things back without a conversation attached.

“Come along, Pipkin,” he rumbled, stones in the voice. Pipkin finished a speck of dust on his flank, bleated once, and trotted to Bor’s side as if the matter were already decided.

“Quiet,” Bor whispered. “As the wind in the obsidian caves.”

Ash dust cushioned their steps until even an ogre of Bor’s size could pretend to be a rumour. Hidden springs warmed the air and sent up puffs that smelled faintly of sulphur, a comfort if you had grown up with it. Hardy flowers — specks of stubborn colour — nodded as if they, too, preferred not to be discussed. Bor kept his head low and his eyes on Grok’s steading, a huddle of dark rock as ancient and weathered as the ridges that owned it. Pipkin walked beside him, an anchor with hooves, fleece taking the last of the light. Who would have thought a peaceful errand could stir such a weather in the belly? Bor would have, actually. He always did. He just hoped the weather would stay indoors.

Dark volcanic dwellings clung to the mountainside. A young ogre stood guard without looming, still in a way that was more work than a roar. This was Stone, Grok’s apprentice. His gaze took attendance.

“Halt,” Stone said, clear and polite. “Who approaches the abode of Elder Ogre Grok?”

Bor’s hands closed. “I am Bor.” Too loud. “This is Pipkin. I have come to return something.” He held out the bloom. It opened a little, greeting the air it had missed.

Stone looked from Bor’s face to the flower and inclined his head, which Bor had not budgeted for. “Bor. Collector of smooth stones, touch like a mountain stream. Pipkin, fleece like dusk gathering. You borrowed the Whispering Bloom.”

Bor blinked. The stones were a private shelf. “Yes. I meant no disrespect. I wanted to admire it. I am returning it before the festival, as I said I would.” His cheeks went the green of embarrassment.

Wind moved the grasses. “Admiration is understandable,” Stone said. “Nobles often take without asking. Your honesty, and your care for what is not yours, is noted.”

Warmth spread through Bor like sun on cool rock. Stone did not demand. He named what he saw and left room around it. Pipkin nudged Bor’s elbow.

“Thank you.” Bor set the bloom in Stone’s hand. Stone took it as if it might bruise.

“Well returned. Your word holds. Enjoy the festival, both of you.”

They walked back lighter. The flutter had become a steady hum. He had been seen, and the seeing had not required a performance.

That evening the Ash Meadow Festival was not grand and did not try to be. Families shared hearty bowls; laughter stitched the cool air; lanterns made a modest gold that turned the grey dust briefly kind. Someone played a pipe that knew only four notes and used them honestly. Children ran until they remembered they were tired. Elder Grok’s beard, at a distance, looked like a piece of the mountain that had decided to attend.

Bor sat with Pipkin by the communal fire, frame unclenched, the empty place in his satchel more comfortable than the flower had been. No one asked him to speak. No one required a story of the borrowing. Stone, across the firelight, raised a cup a fraction; Bor, after a moment, raised his, and the gesture was small enough to survive. Pipkin chewed something he had not been offered and looked, as usual, as if the earth had already explained itself. The bloom, somewhere in Grok’s keeping, would sigh open for the festival and then be itself again. Bor turned a river stone in his pocket — one of the unusually smooth ones — and watched steam from the mountains write a little more twilight. He did not announce what any of it meant. The fire did not ask.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
